hints.junior: Tabbing through the fields in order isn't the same as trapping focus — the boundary where focus tries to leave is the part that actually matters.
hints.mid: "The fields tab through in order" and "focus is trapped inside the dialog" are different claims — a lot of implementations only build the first one.
hints.staff: Reacting to any focus change by yanking it back can fight a screen reader's virtual cursor, which moves independently of DOM focus and doesn't expect the page to fight it.

hints.junior: Open the dialog, then use 'Press Tab' and 'Close dialog' and watch the log and the highlighted element to see exactly where focus moves in each mode.
hints.mid: Broken: Tab on the last field escapes onto the decoy 'page content' element behind the dialog. Fixed: Tab wraps back to the name input, and closing refocuses the trigger.
hints.staff: Both modes call real .focus() on real elements here — this is the actual DOM focus mechanism at work, not an animation standing in for it.

hints.junior: Two obligations: Tab from the last field wraps to the first (and back with Shift+Tab), and closing returns focus to whatever opened the dialog.
hints.mid: Capture Tab at keydown, check the currently focused element against the dialog's focusable-elements list, and explicitly .focus() the wrap target — none of this happens by default.
hints.staff: Computing the focusable-elements list once at dialog-open time goes stale the moment a disabled button becomes enabled or a field appears — recompute it at each Tab press instead.

hints.junior: The native dialog element's showModal() gets you a correct focus trap and Escape-to-close for free, with no hand-written keydown handler.
hints.mid: When hand-rolling is the real constraint, build against the WAI-ARIA APG dialog pattern's exact Tab-wrapping and focus-return requirements, not intuition.
hints.staff: A visual overlay does nothing for the accessibility tree — apply inert (or aria-hidden) to everything outside the dialog, or a screen reader's virtual cursor can still browse through the backdrop.

sections.junior: Today's case is about focus traps in modals — specifically a confirmation dialog that looked keyboard accessible because you could tab through its fields, but was never actually trapping focus at the one moment that mattered.
sections.mid: Tabbing through fields in order and actually trapping focus inside the dialog are two different claims — most modal implementations only build the first one.
sections.staff: The real failure mode is only handling keyboard Tab and nothing else, or worse, fighting a screen reader's own virtual cursor by yanking focus back on a timer.

sections.junior: A correct focus trap does two things. Tab from the last field wraps back to the first instead of leaving the dialog, and closing the dialog returns focus to whatever button opened it, instead of resetting to the top of the page.
sections.mid: Intercept Tab at the boundary with a keydown handler, explicitly call preventDefault and focus, and save the trigger element on open so you can refocus it on close.
sections.staff: The trap breaks in practice when the focusable-elements list is cached once at open time instead of recomputed on every Tab press, so it goes stale the moment the dialog's contents change.

sections.junior: Try opening the dialog and pressing tab past the last field in each mode, then watch where focus actually ends up.
sections.mid: In broken mode, Tab off the Delete button lands on a decoy element behind the dialog. In fixed mode, it wraps back to Name, and closing explicitly refocuses the trigger.
sections.staff: Every focus change here is a real .focus() call on a real element — the only difference between modes is whether a keydown handler intercepts Tab at the boundary.

sections.junior: Fields tabbing through in order is not the same as a real focus trap. Check the boundary: does tab wrap at the ends, and does closing the dialog give focus back to whatever opened it?
sections.mid: Intercept Tab against a freshly computed focusable list, restore focus to the trigger on close, and mark the boundary declaratively with role="dialog" and aria-modal so assistive tech understands it too.
sections.staff: Yanking focus back reactively can fight a screen reader's own virtual cursor — mark the boundary declaratively instead of enforcing it by force.
